newsitem.title: USA: Pathologist in Florida case cites tobacco pressure.
newsitem.headline: Pathologist in Florida case cites tobacco pressure.

text.p: A pathologist who performed years of research funded by the Council for Tobacco Research testified Wednesday that the industry pressured him not to publicise scientific conclusions linking cancer and smoking.

Testifying in a landmark flight attendants case against the cigarette industry, Dr. Freddy Homburger described how another scientist and an attorney told him not to say his research had shown that smoking caused cancer in hamsters.

In a videotaped deposition, he said he was told at a 1973 meeting at his vacation home in Maine that he would receive no more funding from the Council for Tobacco Research if he published a paper using the word "cancer."
Homburger said he initially complied but changed the wording back to his original when the article was sent to him in draft form.
"I believed that the scientific evidence was clearly that cancer had been induced and should therefore not be masqueraded as a more benign situation," he said.

The 81-year-old scientist was called as a witness for plaintiffs in Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al, a $5 billion class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of thousands of flight attendants who say they were sickened by breathing secondhand smoke aboard U.S.-based aircraft.
Now in its third week of testimony, the Dade County Circuit Court case is the first class-action and the first secondhand smoke lawsuit against major cigarette firms to make it to trial.

Homburger also was a witness in a case brought against big tobacco on behalf of Rose Cipollone of New Jersey, a smoker who died of lung cancer. In that case, the first tobacco case reviewed by the Supreme Court, a jury in 1988 awarded the family $400,000. The award was overturned on appeal and the case was eventually dropped.

Earlier Wednesday, Billy Jack Williams, a retired aircraft mechanic and electrician, described how tobacco smoke residue had coated aircraft wires, walls and other components before Congress voted to ban smoking on domestic flights in 1990.

"We used to have to clean it with a couple of cans of aerosol and throw water on it," he said. "... It smelled like tobacco, and if you got it on your hand, (your hand) smelled like tobacco and it was hard to wash off."
Williams said he worked for National Airlines in the 1970s and Pan American World Airways from 1980 to 1991.
Also Wednesday, a cardiologist testified that years of research had convinced him that exposure to secondhand, or environmental, tobacco smoke, made non-smokers sick.

"I don't think there is any significant controversy about whether the effect is there, that is that secondhand smoke causes heart disease," said Dr. John Holbrook, a cardiologist who is chief of the division of general and internal medicine at the University of Utah School of Medicine and has done research for U.S. Surgeon General's reports on smoking.

During cross-examination, David Hardy, an attorney for Philip Morris and Lorillard Inc., asked when Holbrook felt comfortable saying secondhand smoke causes heart disease. Holbrook said he had been convinced by a major study of the effect of secondhand smoke on nurses released this spring.
"Until May 1997, as far as you, Dr. Holbrook, were concerned, there was a real scientific controversy as to whether environmental tobacco smoke causes coronary heart disease," Hardy said.

Holbrook said he disagreed with Hardy's wording. "Up until earlier this year, I considered environmental tobacco smoke to be a major risk factor. ... it's not as if I suddenly changed my mind," he said.

The plaintiffs are expected to present witnesses for about two more weeks. After the plaintiffs rest, attorneys for the tobacco defendants -- Philip Morris Inc., Philip Morris Products Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Lorillard Inc., Lorillard Tobacco Co., Brooke Group Ltd., Liggett Group Inc., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co., the Tobacco Institute and the Council for Tobacco Research -- will present witnesses.
The tobacco defendants say the incidence of lung cancer and other ailments among the flight attendants was no greater than that of other groups of nonsmokers.
Jury selection in the case began June 2.
